passages.t: The lonely city, a widow with no one to comfort her
passages.happening:
The book opens with a cry of shock: “How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!” (verse 1). Jerusalem is pictured as a woman. ‘She who was great among the nations has become a widow’, and ‘The princess of the provinces has become a slave’ (verse 1).

She weeps through the night, and ‘Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her’ (verse 2). Her friends have turned into enemies. Judah has gone into exile and finds no place to rest (verse 3). ‘The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to her appointed feasts’ (verse 4). The gates are empty, the priests groan, and the young women grieve.

The poet names the cause in one line: ‘For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions’ (verse 5). Her children have been taken away as captives. Her princes are like deer with no pasture, too weak to run from the hunter (verse 6). And Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old, while her enemies look on and laugh (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers had seen this. Babylon had besieged Jerusalem for about a year and a half, broken through the wall and burned the temple, the palace and the houses of the city in 587 or 586 BC. Many survivors had been led away to Babylon, and a poorer remnant was left to work the land. The poem does not describe the siege itself. It describes the silence afterward: empty streets, empty roads, festivals no one comes to.

The word ‘How’ is the first word of the book, ekah in Hebrew, and it is the book's Hebrew name. It was the cry that began a funeral song, a cry of shock at the distance between what was and what is. Funerals in Israel included laments, often led by mourning women. This poem takes the funeral song and sings it over a whole city.

A widow in Israel was more than a woman in grief. She often lost her protection, her income and her standing, and the law commanded care for her again and again because she was so exposed. So the picture says Jerusalem has lost everyone who once protected her. Her lovers are probably the allies Judah had trusted, Egypt and the small neighboring kingdoms that had plotted revolt against Babylon with her. None came. Some turned on her.

The poem is an acrostic: its twenty-two stanzas begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order. The form gives a shape to grief that has none, and it suggests grief spoken completely, from first letter to last.
passages.later: The book of Isaiah answers the cry that no one comforts her with the same Hebrew verb: ‘Comfort, comfort My people’ (Isaiah 40:1). Another poem in Isaiah asks the question this chapter raises: ‘Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you?’ (Isaiah 51:19). And a psalm grieves the same ruin: ‘The nations, O God, have invaded Your inheritance; they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble’ (Psalm 79:1).
passages.asks: The poem lets grief speak before it gives any lesson. Ask whether you let your own losses be named before you hurry to explain them. And ask who near you is grieving with no one beside them, the way this city had no one.

passages.t: Jerusalem's sin and shame, and her cry to the LORD
passages.happening:
The narrator says it plainly: ‘Jerusalem has sinned greatly’ (verse 8). Those who once honored her now despise her, and she groans and turns away. Her uncleanness stains her skirts, and she did not think about where her ways would end (verse 9). Her fall was astounding, and again there was no one to comfort her.

Then the city breaks in with a cry of her own: “Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!” (verse 9).

The narrator goes on. ‘The adversary has seized all her treasures’ (verse 10). She has watched foreign nations enter her sanctuary, the very place God had closed to them. Her people groan as they search for bread. ‘They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive’ (verse 11). And the city cries again, ‘Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers knew what the narrator meant by sin. The prophets, Jeremiah above all, had warned for years that the people were breaking their covenant with God, and that siege and exile would follow. The poem does not argue the point. It states it and moves on to the pain.

The pictures in verses 8 and 9 come from two places in Israel's life. One is public shame: to be stripped and exposed was the deepest disgrace. The other is the purity laws, under which certain bodily conditions made a person ritually unclean and set apart from worship for a time. The city that was meant to be holy is now treated as untouchable.

Verse 10 points to the temple. The law kept certain foreigners out of the assembly of the LORD. Now soldiers from the nations have walked into the sanctuary itself and carried off its treasures. Verse 11 fits the famine of the siege and the scarcity that came after it: people traded anything they had for bread.

Notice the two voices. The narrator speaks about the city, and twice the city interrupts with a cry to God. Her words are not polished. She asks only that God would look.
passages.later: The prophets had used the same picture of shame as a warning before the fall: ‘It is because of the magnitude of your iniquity that your skirts have been stripped off and your body has been exposed’ (Jeremiah 13:22). Later, God speaks to the city as one whose shame will be taken away: ‘No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate’ (Isaiah 62:4).
passages.hard:
The poem pictures Jerusalem as a woman who is exposed, stained and despised. How should a reader take that picture?

The prophets often spoke of a city as a woman, the Daughter of Zion, and spoke of its disgrace in the language of a woman's public shame. In this poem the woman is the city, and the shame is the city's fall: its walls broken, its temple entered, its people taken. The picture belongs to a poem about a nation and its covenant with God. Notice too that the poem does not mock her. The narrator grieves for her, and in the next verses she speaks for herself.

This is a prophetic picture of a city. It gives no warrant to any man to shame or harm a woman, and it is not a description of how any woman should be treated.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The city's prayer is short: she asks God only to look. Ask whether you have ever felt too ashamed to pray more than that, and whether you believe God hears so short a prayer. And ask where you have traded what was precious just to get through a hard season.

passages.t: Is there any sorrow like hers?
passages.happening:
Now the city speaks for herself. She calls to everyone who walks past: “Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see!” (verse 12). She asks whether there is ‘any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger’ (verse 12).

She describes what God has done. He sent fire into her bones, spread a net for her feet, and left her faint all day (verse 13). Her transgressions are bound into a yoke and laid on her neck (verse 14). The Lord has rejected her mighty men and summoned an army to crush her young warriors. He has trampled her like grapes in a winepress (verse 15).

‘For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears’ (verse 16). There is no one nearby to comfort her or revive her, and her children are destitute.

The narrator breaks in for one verse: ‘Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her’ (verse 17). The LORD has turned her neighbors into her foes, and Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them.
passages.hearers:
The city calls to the travelers who pass her ruins, as a mourner might call to people passing a house of grief. In Israel, friends came to sit with the bereaved. Jerusalem has only strangers walking past.

The yoke of verse 14 was the wooden bar laid on the necks of oxen, a common picture of subjection. Here the city's own sins have become the yoke. The word for transgression, pesha, means a deliberate breach of a covenant, not a mistake. The city does not pretend she is innocent. She carries the weight of what she did.

The winepress of verse 15 was where grapes were trodden underfoot. It is one of the most violent pictures in the poem, and the city says the Lord himself did the treading.

The refrain that there is no one to comfort comes twice in these verses (verses 16 and 17). It runs through the whole chapter five times, and it builds toward the plea that the LORD himself would look.
passages.later: In Isaiah, the LORD answers a city who said she was forgotten: ‘Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?’ (Isaiah 49:15). And the prophet Jeremiah wept over the same people in words close to verse 16: ‘My eyes overflow with tears; day and night they do not cease’ (Jeremiah 14:17).
passages.asks: The city asks the passers-by whether her sorrow means nothing to them. Ask whose grief you walk past without stopping. And ask what it would look like to sit with one person this week, as Israel's mourners sat with the bereaved, without trying to fix anything.

passages.t: Zion confesses, and prays for justice
passages.happening:
The city confesses: ‘The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against His command’ (verse 18). She asks all peoples to look at her suffering. Her young men and young women have gone into captivity.

She called to her lovers, and they betrayed her. Her priests and elders died in the city while they searched for food to stay alive (verse 19). Then she turns to God: “See, O LORD, how distressed I am!” (verse 20). She is churning inside. Outside, the sword takes her children. Inside, there is death.

People have heard her groaning, but there is no one to comfort her (verse 21). Her enemies have heard of her trouble and are glad that God has caused it. So she prays that the day God has announced would come for them too, that they would become like her. ‘Let all their wickedness come before You, and deal with them as You have dealt with me because of all my transgressions’ (verse 22). The poem ends with her groans and her faint heart.
passages.hearers:
Confession and grief stand side by side here. The city says God is right, and in the same breath she asks him to see how much it hurts. The first hearers had heard prophets promise that the fall would not come. Now it had come, and they needed words that admitted their guilt without pretending the pain was small.

The priests and elders dying while they searched for food points to the famine of the siege.

The enemies who were glad were the nations around Judah. The prophets later condemn Edom in particular for gloating over Jerusalem's fall and joining the plunder. The city's last prayer asks God to deal with them as he has dealt with her. It is a prayer for equal justice, and it hands that justice to God rather than taking it into her own hands.

The chapter ends without comfort. That is deliberate. The poem has given grief its full say before the book goes on.
passages.later: A psalm of the same ruin prays, ‘How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?’ (Psalm 79:5). The prophet Obadiah condemns Edom for the gladness this verse describes: ‘you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune’ (Obadiah 1:12). And Paul tells believers not to take revenge but to ‘leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard:
If Jerusalem admits her sin, why does she still ask God to punish her enemies?

Some readers find the prayer vindictive. Others see a sense of justice in it. The nations that destroyed Jerusalem were not innocent tools. They acted with cruelty and were glad of her ruin, and if God judges his own people for sin, he must also judge theirs. On this reading the prayer asks for equal justice, and it hands that justice to God instead of seeking revenge.

It is also the prayer of someone in extreme pain. The Bible records such prayers honestly without approving every feeling in them. The New Testament adds Jesus' command, ‘love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you’ (Matthew 5:44), and it also says that God will judge justly (Romans 12:19). Both belong in the reader's mind when this verse is prayed.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The city confesses her own wrong and still asks for justice on those who wronged her. Ask whether you can hold both: honesty about your own part, and a refusal to call cruelty done to you right. And ask what it would mean to hand your anger to God rather than act on it.
